newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Africans, France dig in heels on Boutros - Ghali.
newsitem.headline: Africans, France dig in heels on Boutros - Ghali.

text.p: In defiance of the U.S. veto against the re-election of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, African nations on Monday did not budge from supporting the 74-year-old Egyptian law professor.

"We don't have any (new) list. It is composed of one person, Dr. Boutros-Ghali," said Botswana's U.N. ambassador Legwaila Joseph Legwaila, a member of the 15-seat Security Council which makes the decision.

For many African countries, a united front was a mark of achievement that was difficult to obtain and may be difficult to sustain. Their first satisfaction, they say, was last Tuesday's 14-1 vote in the Security Council which diplomatically isolated the United States.

On the other hand, several Security Council nations, including Britain, would probably abstain if the vote on Boutros-Ghali was taken again, mainly because they have accepted the fact that the United States will not change its mind. However, France, Russia and China, who also have veto power on the council, are still backing Boutros-Ghali.

Some African nations have candidates they want to promote for the job -- the only woman considered so far was Mozambique's former first lady, Gracia Macel, an education specialist, who has said she was not interested.

But they have been told to hold back on making a formal proposal until they are convinced there is no hope of negotiating at least a two-year extension for Boutros-Ghali. Diplomats say they have also been told France might veto any nomination at this time.
Paul Biya, head of the Organisation of African Unity, is expected to telephone heads of African nations this week but no one expects a quick reply from 52 members.

Boutros-Ghali's term runs out at the end of this year, and the council has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if he is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.
Still in the background of the African strategy is France, which is expected to make sure no candidate seriously challenged Boutros-Ghali in the next week or so.

"The French want to prevent agreement on anyone else and then have members go on bended knee to (President Bill) Clinton and say there is no way forward except a compromise," said one Security Council envoy. So far there is no sign Washington would even consider a two-year compromise after Boutros-Ghali last spring turned down its offer of a one-year extension.

France's second strategy, some diplomats say, is to delay until there is unanimity among Francophone African nations on a candidate, a position criticised by the French daily Le Monde as dividing African nations unnecessarily and using the "impeccable mastery of the language of Moliere" as a prime criteria.
But several council members are unhappy about the deadlock and want the 15-seat body to move forward quickly.
One plan was for Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia to present a list between now and the end of the month comprised of every candidate mentioned in the press or among diplomats.
The danger of this procedure for the Africans is that names from other regions would be mentioned. Asian candidates are thought to have the best chance if no one can agree on an African.

The United States says Boutros-Ghali has spent too little time streamlining the bodies, and the progress that has been made is due solely to U.S. pressure. More realistically, Washington says it cannot get the $1.4 billion it owes to the United Nations from a Republican-dominated Congress while he is in office.
